title: EFFECT OF DIFFERENT SUTURE MATERIALS AND TECHNIQUES ON GASTRIC WALL TISSUE HEALING IN GASTROTOMY SURGERY IN DOGS
text: EFFECT OF DIFFERENT SUTURE MATERIALS AND TECHNIQUES ON GASTRIC WALL TISSUE HEALING IN GASTROTOMY SURGERY IN DOGS.  The article investigates the effect of different suturing techniques and suture materials used to close surgical wounds of the gastric wall during gastrotomy on the wound-healing process. The study was conducted at the Veterinary Clinic of Tashkent State Agrarian University and involved gastrotomy procedures performed on six dogs of different breeds diagnosed with pathological conditions associated with gastric lesions or foreign body ingestion. The animals were divided into two groups of three dogs each. In the first group, the gastric wound was closed using a two-layer suture technique consisting of Schmieden and Lambert sutures with synthetic lavsan suture material. In the second group, the wound was closed using a single-layer seromuscular Lambert suture with silk suture material. During the postoperative period, the general condition, appetite, behavior, defecation, and local condition of the surgical wound were monitored. The wound condition was assessed on days 5 and 10 after surgery. According to the observations, the group in which the two-layer Schmieden–Lambert suture technique and synthetic lavsan material were used developed a relatively smooth and firm scar. In contrast, the group treated with a single-layer Lambert suture and silk material showed a relatively coarse scar with localized areas of prominence. The practical findings of the study were also supported by clinical cases observed in veterinary clinics in Kibray, Tashkent District, and Chirchiq.

title: EFFECTIVENESS OF THE IMMUNOCORRECTION-DEWORMING-VACCINATION CHAIN BASED ON THE DOSTIM IMMUNOCORRECTOR IN THE PREVENTION OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES IN SERVICE DOGS
journal: Abduraxmonov Sanjar, Abduraupova Shahrizoda, Ulmasov Botir
text: EFFECTIVENESS OF THE IMMUNOCORRECTION-DEWORMING-VACCINATION CHAIN BASED ON THE DOSTIM IMMUNOCORRECTOR IN THE PREVENTION OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES IN SERVICE DOGS.  The effectiveness of organizing the prevention of infectious diseases in young service-dog puppies on the basis of an immunocorrection-deworming-vaccination sequence was evaluated. A total of 16 puppies were included in the study, and four groups were formed according to breed: Labrador, Belgian Shepherd, German Shepherd, and Cocker Spaniel. Each group contained 2 experimental and 2 control animals. In the experimental groups, Dostim was administered at a dose of 0.4-0.6 mL for 1-5 kg of live body weight, three times at 3-day intervals. Five days later, Adjipras and Azinox Plus were given at a dose of 1 tablet per 10 kg of live body weight, twice at 14-day intervals, after which Multican-5 vaccination was performed. Clinical observation was conducted for 21 days after vaccination. The same regimen was maintained in the control groups, except that Dostim was not administered. Various clinical signs were recorded in the control animals, whereas none were observed in the experimental animals treated with Dostim. The results indicate a positive clinical trend associated with the immunocorrection stage in this preventive chain.

title: In vivo Study of the Effect of Composition and Implantation Site on Scaffold Degradation Rate: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) 50:50+20wt%TaOx, Intraperitoneal
journal: Hix, Jeremy M.L., Troia, Arianna, Shapiro, Erik
text:
In vivo Study of the Effect of Composition and Implantation Site on Scaffold Degradation Rate: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) 50:50+20wt%TaOx, Intraperitoneal.  Tissue engineering devices stabilize wounds, then degrade. However, published degradation rates often conflict.   Incorporating monitoring functionality into devices allows real-time assessment of degradation and failure, but requires contrast agents, as polymer devices are invisible to most medical imaging modalities. Therefore, computed tomography (CT)-visible composite scaffolds were created from 5-20 wt% tantalum oxide (TaO x ) nanoparticles in polymers with distinct degradation profiles: polycaprolactone, poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) 85:15 and PLGA 50:50, representing slow, medium and fast degrading materials. Scaffolds, mimicking biomedical devices, were implanted into mice intramuscularly or intraperitoneally, and monitored via CT over 20 weeks. Scaffold degradation profile was dictated by polymer matrix, regardless of nanoparticle addition. Foreign body response was dependent on implant site and in mid-degrading composites degradation rates transitioned from linear degradation intramuscularly to exponential degradation intraperitoneally. Nanoparticle excretion via liver and spleen lagged polymer degradation. Overall, real time tracking of device behavior was demonstrated, advancing an era of personalized medicine. Published as: Pawelec, K.M., Hix, J.M.L., Troia, A.  et al.  In vivo study of the effect of composition and implantation site on scaffold degradation rate.  Commun Mater  (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-026-01308-5 
 This dataset contains longitudinal microCT scans of poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) 50:50+20wt% TaOx, implanted intraperitoneally. Each individual in the group (n=6) was scanned 25 mm field of view (4 min total scan time) at 50 μm resolution, centered on the implanted scaffold. After all acquisitions, individual scaffolds were again sub-reconstructed using the Quantum GX software to 12 µm resolution.

title: Traditional and Modern Techniques for Propensity Score Estimation in Clinical Trials
journal: Lee, Kangwoo, Mares, Jennifer, Jiang, Songtao
text: Traditional and Modern Techniques for Propensity Score Estimation in Clinical Trials.  Propensity scores (PS) are central to causal inference in observational studies, but their reliability depends on the modeling strategy used to estimate them. Statistical models such as logistic regression remain common for their interpretability, while machine-learning methods offer more flexibility for capturing nonlinear and high-dimensional relationships. Yet how these approaches affect causal effect estimation is not well understood. In this study, we compare PS estimates from multiple algorithms across two categories: (1) parametric statistical models and (2) non-parametric machine-learning methods. We provide a broad comparison of how different modeling approaches influence estimated propensity scores and the resulting balance between groups. We also highlight general factors that may contribute to variation across methods.

title: Boundary-Relative Statehood and Top-Down Causality in Statistical Mechanics and Gibbs Thermodynamics: An Exact Enclosing-Reversal Theorem
text: Boundary-Relative Statehood and Top-Down Causality in Statistical Mechanics and Gibbs Thermodynamics: An Exact Enclosing-Reversal Theorem.   Statistical mechanics is conventionally interpreted bottom-up, but its count structure determines statistical direction before microscopic occurrence enters the description. We prove the opposite causal ordering from the count structure itself. Defining microstates and macrostates relative to a count boundary separates possible structure from its realization. Native multiplicity is fixed by the boundary-defined state space, while compatible enclosing multiplicity supplies an independent directional relation. Together they completely determine pre-realization statistical direction; subordinate occurrence contributes no independent directional term. We further prove that enclosing compatibility can exactly reverse the native local direction while the local multiplicity landscape remains unchanged. Thus statistical directional causality is necessarily top-down, while microscopic processes locally realize that direction. Finally, we prove the thermodynamic mapping,   showing that Gibbs reaction direction is the thermodynamic realization of the same causal structure. Bottom-up microscopic occurrence is therefore not the source of statistical or Gibbs thermodynamic direction.

In vitro transfer dynamics of extended-spectrum β-lactamases from human and canine-derived E. coli to commensal Enterobacteriaceae
journal: Whitehead-Tillery, Charles E., Waite, Samantha E., Snowden, Samuel J.
text:
In vitro transfer dynamics of extended-spectrum β-lactamases from human and canine-derived E. coli to commensal Enterobacteriaceae.   Abstract  
  Background/Objectives:  
 Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing  Enterobacteriaceae  represents a serious public health threat, compromising treatment options for infections in both humans and dogs. Dogs have been suggested as potential contributors to ESBL dissemination in the community via horizontal gene transfer (HGT) due to their close contact with humans and ability to act as community reservoirs that harbor ESBL-producing bacteria. However, it is unknown whether ESBL-producing bacteria from dogs can successfully transfer β-lactamase genes to human bacteria especially those in the gut microbiota. Moreover, the frequency at which plasmids harboring β-lactamase genes transfer even under controlled  in vitro  conditions remains poorly understood. This study aimed to determine the  in vitro  transfer frequencies of β-lactamase genes associated with ESBLs from human- and dog-derived  Escherichia coli  ( E. coli ) to a human commensal recipient, and, where transfer occurred, to assess the recipient’s capacity to disseminate β-lactamase genes to other gut bacteria. 
     
  Methods:  
 Donor strains included uropathogenic  E. coli  (UPEC) from humans and dogs with urinary tract infections (UTIs) carrying cefotaxime resistance. The primary recipient we used was a human-derived  E. coli  LM715 strain which harbored a chromosomal red fluorescent protein along with kanamycin ( kanR ) and chloramphenicol ( chlR ) resistance markers. Secondary recipients tested were gut-associated recipient strains including  E. coli  MG1655,  Klebsiella pneumoniae, Citrobacter rodentium , and  Salmonella enterica  each carrying rifampicin resistance on the chromosome. We performed  in vitro  filter matings to determine the transfer frequency of β-lactamase-associated resistance using antibiotic selective media. DNA extractions were performed on a subset of donors and transconjugants to evaluate the presence of transferred β-lactamase genes. Subsequently, we conducted a secondary transfer in which  E. coli  LM715 recipients that acquired CTX resistance were transferred to many different enteric bacteria including  E. coli  MG1655,  K. pneumoniae ,  C. rodentium , and  S. enterica . Whole-genome sequencing of a subset of donors and transconjugants confirmed the presence of β-lactamase genes in  E. coli  LM715 consistent with donor-derived resistance supporting horizontal gene transfer. 
   
  Results  
 Human- and dog-derived UPEC** strains successfully transferred CTX resistance to  E. coli  LM715 in the primary transfer experiments at detectable frequencies. Measured transfer frequencies varied across isolates, with notable differences between human-and dog-derived donors indicating that some recipients were more permissive to transfers. We also observed transfer frequencies from LM715 to gut-associated bacteria which demonstrated the potential for commensal bacterial strains in the gut microbiota to act as reservoirs for β-lactamase dissemination. 
   
  Conclusions  
 These studies demonstrate that β-lactam resistance can be disseminated between human- and dog-derived  E. coli  and across diverse  Enterobacteriaceae  under  in vitro  conditions. From a One Health perspective these findings highlight the potential role of dogs as reservoirs for β-lactam resistance and support the possibility of gut commensals from humans and dogs contributing to ESBL dissemination.

title: REGEN-X: A Closed-Loop Bioresorbable Regenerative Scaffold for Patient-Specific Healing Monitoring and Adaptive Local Therapy
text: REGEN-X: A Closed-Loop Bioresorbable Regenerative Scaffold for Patient-Specific Healing Monitoring and Adaptive Local Therapy.  REGEN-X is a conceptual closed-loop bioresorbable regenerative scaffold designed to integrate multimodal biosensing, patient-specific healing-state estimation, trajectory-based monitoring, confidence-aware decision logic, and adaptive local therapeutic control. The proposed system aims to continuously characterize the local regenerative environment and adapt therapeutic activity according to deviations from an expected healing trajectory. This manuscript presents the system architecture, methodology, proposed control framework, validation strategy, limitations, and future research directions. The work is conceptual and does not report human or animal clinical results.

Pham on June 17, 2023, from the same locality as ZMMU Re-18512; • Dak Lak Province: Chu Yang Sin NP: ZMMU Re-14068 (field tag NAP-02669), adult male, collected from polydominant mixed evergreen montane forests on the slope of Mt. Chu Pan Fan, within the Chu Yang Sin NP, Bong Krang Commune (12.37557°N, 108.354057°E; elevation 1,730 m asl) by N. A. Poyarkov on 07 April 2012.   Referred material   (n = 2, all from Vietnam). • Lam Dong Province: Sui Kat area, D’Ran Commune: NHMUK 1921.5. 4.11, adult male, collected by Malcolm Smith in 1921. • Khanh Hoa Province: Hon Ba NR: ZMMU Re-15709, subadult female, collected by A. B. Vassilleva on 29 June 2018 (12.11250°N, 108.97889°E; elevation 800 m asl).   Diagnosis.    Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. can be distinguished from all other congeners by the following combination of characters: (1) TaL / TL ratio 0.14–0.18 in males and 0.12–0.14 in females; (2) internasals usually in contact, rarely separated by one small scale; (3) second supralabial bordering loreal pit; (4) dorsal scale rows 25 (21, 23, 27) – 21 (23, 25) – 19 (15, 17); (5) ventrals 129–138; (6) dorsal scales strongly keeled; (7) subcaudals 36–44, all single; (8) fourth supralabial larger than third; (9) dorsal surface of head uniformly dark brown to blackish-brown, lacking distinct markings; (10) sides of head heavily mottled with cream and pale orange; (11) a pair of pale dorsolateral neck stripes present; (12) dorsum yellowish-brown to brown, with a series of dark brown to blackish-brown butterfly-shaped, subquadrate, or irregular blotches; (13) tail brown, bearing scattered whitish spots; and (14) venter cream to off-white, densely mottled with dark brown.   Description of holotype.   Adult male (Figs 5, 6 A), specimen in good condition.   Morphology . Body stout and robust; SVL 298 mm, TaL 50 mm, TL 348 mm, TaL / TL ratio 0.14. Head distinctly triangular in dorsal view, clearly differentiated from neck; HL 16.96 mm, HL / SVL ratio 0.06. Snout blunt and rounded, rostral small, trapezoidal, broader than high, barely visible from above; canthus rostralis indistinct. Eyes small; ED 2.36 mm, SnL 5.08 mm, SnL / ED ratio 2.15. Pupil vertically elliptic.   Head scalation . Loreal pit large, deep, triangular. Nostril situated within a large undivided nasal scale. First supralabial separated from nasal by a distinct suture. Second supralabial forming the anterior border of the loreal pit. Preoculars 3 / 3; postoculars 3 / 3. Subocular 1 / 1; subocular separated from the supralabials by one row of small scales. Loreal single. Supralabials 8 / 8, fourth supralabial distinctly larger than third and fifth; infralabials 10 / 10, first pair contacting each other behind mental, first to third in contact with chin shields; mental triangular; one pair of chin shields, meeting in midline. Internasals large, in broad medial contact, not separated by small scales. Supraoculars large, single on each side. Scales on dorsal surface of snout and interorbital region smooth, irregularly arranged; temporal and occipital scales smooth.   Body scalation . Dorsal scale rows 25–21 – 19, distinctly keeled except for the outermost row, which is smooth. Ventrals 130; preventrals 1. Cloacal plate entire. Subcaudals 37, all single.   Hemipenes . The hemipenes are incompletely everted  in situ  (Fig. 6). The exposed portions are short and stout and densely covered with spinulate calyces. Because the organs are incompletely everted, the morphology of the lobes and apical ornamentation could not be reliably assessed. In preservative, the hemipenes are pale pink to translucent white.   Coloration in life    (Figs 5, 7 A) . Dorsal surface of head uniformly dark brown to blackish-brown, lacking distinct dorsal markings. Rostral region, supralabials, preocular, postocular, and temporal regions heavily ornamented with cream and pale orange spots and vermiculations, forming a conspicuous mottled pattern on the sides of the head. A pair of narrow pale cream dorsolateral stripes extends from the posterior margin of the head onto the neck. Iris dark grayish-brown with a vertically elliptical pupil. Dorsal ground coloration of body dark brown to grayish brown, with a series of large pale tan to yellowish-brown blotches, mostly butterfly-shaped to subquadrate and separated by broad dark interspaces; the blotches become smaller and less distinct posteriorly. Tail dark brown, bearing scattered cream to whitish spots. Ventral surface cream to off-white, densely mottled with dark brown blotches and speckles, forming irregular transverse markings along the body and tail; chin and throat predominantly cream with scattered dark brown markings.   Variation   (for detailed information, see Table 1, Fig. 7). The longest known specimen is 474 mm long (SVL 406 mm, TaL 68 mm; adult female, ZMMU Re-13839); the longest known male is 463 mm long (SVL 379 mm, TaL 84 mm; ZMMU Re-14068). Ratio TaL / TL: 0.12–0.18 (0.14–0.18 in males, 0.12–0.14 in females).   Body scalation . DSR 25 (21, 23, 27) – 21 (23, 25) – 19 (15, 17); VEN 129–138; SC 36–44.   Head scalation . SL 8 (rarely 9); IL: 9 (rarely 10); InN-sep 0 (rarely 1); CEP 5–7; He-SC 18–22.   Coloration and pattern . Dorsal ground coloration varies from yellowish-brown to brown. The dorsal blotches are dark brown to blackish-brown and vary from butterfly-shaped to subquadrate or irregular in shape. They also vary in size, degree of fusion, and contrast with the ground coloration. The dorsal surface of the head is generally uniform dark brown to blackish-brown; however, the extent of pale mottling on the lateral surfaces of the head varies among individuals. Cream and pale orange markings on the supralabial, preocular, postocular, and temporal regions range from sparse and fragmented to extensive, forming conspicuous reticulations. The pale dorsolateral stripes on the neck are usually distinct but may vary in width and intensity. The tail bears scattered cream to whitish spots, which vary in size and prominence among specimens. Ventral coloration ranges from cream to grayish-white and is variably mottled with dark brown; the mottling may be sparse and scattered or dense, forming irregular transverse markings on the ventral surfaces of the body and tail. Live specimens generally exhibit warmer coloration, with yellowish-brown to orange-brown dorsal hues and more conspicuous cream to pale orange markings on the sides of the head than preserved specimens.   Etymology.   The specific epithet “  langbianus  ” is a masculine Latin adjective derived from the name of the Langbian Plateau, the broader geographic region containing the type locality and the currently known distribution of the new species. The name highlights the biogeographic isolation of the Langbian Plateau, an important center of montane endemism in Indochina. We suggest the following common names for the new species: “ Langbian Mountain Pitviper ” (in English), “ R ắn l ục núi Langbian ” (in Vietnamese), “ Лангбианский горный щитомордник ” (Langbianskiy gornyi schitomordnik, in Russian), and “ Ovophis de Langbian ” (in French).   Comparisons.   The main diagnostic characters separating  Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. from its congeners are summarized in Table 2. Morphologically,  Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. most closely resembles  O. tonkinensis . It can be distinguished from the latter by its smaller adult body size (maximum SVL 379 mm in males and 406 mm in females vs. 477 mm in males and 563 mm in females); lower TaL / TL ratio in males (0.14–0.18 [mean 0.16] vs. 0.18–0.21 [mean 0.19]); fewer subcaudals in males (SC 37–44 [mean 38.8] vs. 47–55 [mean 51.1]); absence or rare occurrence of small scales separating the internasals (usually absent, rarely one vs. usually one or two); fewer He-SC (18–21 [mean 19.6] in males and 21–22 [mean 21.7] in females vs. 25–32 [mean 27.6] in males and 25–31 [mean 28.6] in females); fewer infralabials in males (IL 9–10 vs. 10–12); and fewer supralabials (SL 8, rarely 9 vs. 9–10).   Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. further differs from  O. anitae ,  O. convictus ,  O. jenkinsi ,  O. monticola ,  O. medogensis , and  O. zhaoermii  by having undivided subcaudals (vs. paired or predominantly paired). It is additionally distinguished from these species by the fourth supralabial being larger than the third (vs. the third supralabial larger and taller than the fourth). The new species differs from  O. makazayazaya  by possessing undivided subcaudals (vs. paired or predominantly paired) and fewer supralabials (8, rarely 9 vs. 10–11, rarely 9 or 12).  Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. differs from  O. zayuensis , which also has undivided subcaudals, in having the fourth supralabial larger than the third (vs. the third supralabial larger and taller than the fourth), and fewer ventrals (129–136 in males, 132–138 in females vs. 162–176 in males, 160–175 in females).   Distribution and natural history.    Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. is currently known only from the Langbian Plateau of southern Vietnam, where it has been recorded from several localities: Bidoup-Nui Ba NP as well as Di Linh and D’Ran Communes in Lam Dong Province (with additional observations from Da Lat Commune; T. V. Nguyen, pers. obs.), Chu Yang Sin NP in Dak Lak Province, and Hon Ba NR in Khanh Hoa Province (Fig. 1).  The species inhabits montane tropical evergreen forests at moderate to high elevations from 800 to 2,230 m asl. At these localities, the new species was recorded in different types of forests ranging from highly disturbed secondary montane polydominant, evergreen forests or pine forests dominated by  Pinus kesiya  Royle ex Gordon and  P. dalatensis  Ferré (family Pinaceae Lindley) at lower elevations to high-elevation elfin montane forests composed of trees from the families Fagaceae Dumort., Lauraceae Juss., and Magnoliaceae Juss., characterized by a thick leaf litter layer, numerous fallen logs, and numerous streams.  Ovophis langbianus  sp. nov. is a nocturnal species, typically active between 19: 00 and 23: 00 h. Individuals have been observed on the forest floor among leaf litter, usually in the vicinity of streams. Occasionally, specimens were found under fallen logs; the female specimen ZMMU Re-13839 was found inside the decayed heartwood of a large fallen log. Sympatric pitviper species include  Trimeresurus albolabris fario  (Jan, 1859),  T. rubeus  (Malhotra, Thorpe, Mrinalini & Stuart, 2011), and  T. vogeli  David, Vidal & Pauwels, 2001.   Conservation status.   At present, no major threats have been documented for the new species. However, individuals are occasionally killed by local people because of their venomous nature or by vehicles while crossing roads (T. V. Nguyen, pers. obs.). Habitat loss and forest degradation may represent localized threats, particularly in the Di Linh Commune, Lam Dong Province, Vietnam. Because information on population size, population trends, and reproductive biology remains unavailable, a formal conservation assessment is premature. Nevertheless, given its apparently broad distribution across the Langbian Plateau and occurrence within several protected areas, we tentatively recommend that  O. langbianus  sp. nov. be classified as Least Concern (LC) according to the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria (IUCN Standards and Petitions Subcommittee 2019).

title: napari: a multi-dimensional image viewer for Python

text:
napari: a multi-dimensional image viewer for Python.  napari 0.9.0 
  Tue, Aug 25, 2026  
 We're happy to announce the release of napari 0.9.0!
napari is a fast, interactive, multi-dimensional image viewer for Python.
It's designed for browsing, annotating, and analyzing large multi-dimensional
images. It's built on top of Qt (for the GUI), vispy (for performant GPU-based
rendering), and the scientific Python stack (numpy, scipy). 
 For more information, examples, and documentation, please visit our website,
https://napari.org. 
 napari follows  EffVer (Intended Effort Versioning) ; this is a  Macro  release containing awesome new features, but may require dedication of some significant time when upgrading projects to use this version. 
 Highlights 
 Auto-labelling of viewer axes 
 napari 0.5.0 laid the ground work for more accurate metadata handling by
allowing users and plugins to set the  axis_labels  on layers. napari 0.9.0
 finally  capitalises on that work by automatically labelling viewer axes based
on the axis labels of layers present in the viewer.
( #9282 ) 
 Now, opening a dataset with labelled axes will result in correctly labelled
axes in the viewer: 
  
 Additionally, when you create a new layer from an existing one using the
buttons in the GUI, the new layer now inherits the axis labels of the layer(s)
it was derived from. ( #9293 ) 
 There is still work to be done here. For example, if layers have labels that
are inconsistent with each other, napari will simply ignore layers with fewer
dimensions, or layers added later. But, for most use cases, layer and viewer
metadata will now be much more informative! 
 Xarray metadata is now inherited 
 In the same vein, if you work with  Xarray  — common in climate,
geoscience, and many places where data ships with labelled coordinates — napari
now reads metadata straight from your  DataArray s. When you add an xarray
object to the viewer, napari will use its dimension names as axis labels, infer
 scale  and  translate  from the coordinate values, and pick up  units  from
CF-convention  units  attributes on coordinates ( #9316 ).
This closed an 8-year old, double-digit, nearly-as-old-as-napari-itself issue!
( #14 ) 
 Status bar coordinates as floats 
 Continuing on the theme of improved metadata, when scale and/or unit metadata
is set on the layer, the status bar coordinates now have increased precision,
where before they were limited to just integers. This means you can have more
accurate physical estimates of your data coordinates when exploring data.
( #9287 ) 
 Layer controls for multiple selected layers 
 Until now, layer controls only appeared when a single layer was selected. Now,
napari dynamically builds the layer controls from your selection, so
when you select several layers at once you can see and use the controls that
are shared between them. Pan-zoom is always available, while the layer-specific
buttons still appear only when a single layer is selected.

 There's also an experimental setting,  Generate GUI layer controls dynamically
instead of using premade panels , that makes napari use the new dynamic
controls even for single layers. 
 Take a guided tour of the viewer 
 New to napari, or just want a quick refresher on where everything lives? There's
now a guided tour, available from  Help → Take a tour . The tour highlights
the main areas of the viewer — the canvas, the layer list, layer controls, the
viewer buttons, the dimension sliders, and the status bar — so you can get your
bearings in seconds. If the viewer is empty, napari opens the built-in  Balls
(3D)  sample data so the walkthrough has something to show ( #9290 ). 
 ![Screenshot of the napari viewer guided tour][../_static/images/guided-tour.png) 
 Contributable plugin preferences 
 Plugins can now ship their own preferences ( #9308 )!
By declaring  configurations  in
their  napari.yaml  manifest, plugins get their own settings — stored
separately from napari's own settings, automatically added to and editable from
the napari  Preferences  dialog, and accessible programmatically from Python: 
  from napari.settings import get_plugin_settings

settings = get_plugin_settings("my-plugin")
settings.reader.lazy = True
  
 Read more in the  Configurations Guide 
to learn more about how to add this new contribution to your own plugins. 
 Adjust grid rendering with hidden layers 
 Grid mode with hidden layers is much improved: empty
grid spaces are never shown and stride operates on the  full  layer list, so
layer grouping doesn't change when you show or hide layers ( #9244 ). 
 Fuzzy find in command palette 
 Have you used our  command palette  yet? It's a great way to
quickly access and even discover napari functionality. Now, thanks to
 #8661 , it's easier to find
functions when you don't know the exact name, or you mistyped something. You'll
need to have  rapidfuzz  installed to
make use of it. It's automatically installed with  napari[all]  or
 napari[optional] . And if the search feels a bit off, you can set just how
fuzzy you want it to be in Preferences > Experimental > Fuzzy Search Threshold. 
  
 2D slicing of surfaces 
 Ever since we added surfaces, they have been invisible in 2D slices. Now,
thanks to all the work done on  thick slicing , surface
slices appear in 2D view ( #8783 ).
This enhancement is accompanied by support for async slicing, which should
improve viewer responsiveness when slicing large, time varying surfaces, for
example.

  <video width="100%" controls autoplay loop muted playsinline>
    <source src="../_static/images/slicing_surface.webm" type="video/webm" />
    <source src="../_static/images/slicing_surface.mp4" type="video/mp4" />
    <img src="../_static/images/slicing_surface.png"
      title="Your browser does not support the video tag"
      alt="Video showing a slicing of surface layers, with showing how to change thickness of slize and controlling slice mmode."
    >
  </video>
</figure>
  
 ... And you can try this out yourself with common .obj surface files thanks to
a new built-in reader plugin!
( #9228 ) 
 You should now be able to drag and drop .obj files into napari and see them
instantly. 
 Public API for auto contrast limits 
 For a very long time, it's been possible to set automatic contrast limits
updating on a layer  only  through the graphical user interface. This means an
extra click for many workflows and poorer reproducibility. Thanks to
 #9271 , you can now set the
 auto_contrast  attribute on Image layers: 
  image_layer = viewer.add_image(..., auto_contrast=True)
# or
image_layer.auto_contrast = True
  
 The life-changing magic of tidying up the Viewer model 
 The napari Viewer model, for historical reasons, is a grab-bag of  many 
attributes, which makes usage, discoverability, and code modularity and
composability a major issue. We've taken some  big  steps towards cleaning up
one of our most important namespaces by creating Canvas
( #8633 ) and Scene
( #9323 ) models, which cleans up
( #9363 ) and clarifies
( napari/docs#1083 ) many parts of
the API. 
 The old API is in extremely widespread use, so although it is silently
deprecated, it will continue to work for the foreseeable future. In the
meantime, the new API should be much friendlier to work with by carefully
grouping related concepts and APIs. Some examples: 
 
  viewer.axes  and  viewer.floating_axes  become  viewer.scene.overlays.axes 
and  viewer.canvas.overlays.axes . 
 From that API, you may also guess that the scale bar is on
 viewer.canvas.overlays.scale_bar . 
 You can even get a list of the current overlays (both visible and invisible)
with  list(viewer.canvas.overlays)  and  list(viewer.scene.overlays) . (But
do note that overlays with a  _  prefix are private and may change!) 
  viewer.camera  is now  viewer.scene.camera . 
 Grid mode is now accessed at  viewer.canvas.grid  (e.g.
 viewer.canvas.grid.enabled = True ). 
 
 This has also enabled a new public API: you can now query the canvas size (in
pixels) without accessing private napari APIs! Check  viewer.canvas.size ! 
 The TL;DR: 
  # Canvas Model
viewer.scale_bar -> viewer.canvas.overlays.scale_bar
viewer.text_overlay -> viewer.canvas.overlays.text
viewer.floating_axes -> viewer.canvas.overlays.axes
viewer.grid -> viewer.canvas.grid
NOW EXPOSED -> viewer.canvas.overlays.current_slice
NEW -> viewer.canvas.overlay_tiling
NEW -> viewer.canvas.background_color & viewer.canvas.background_color_override
NEW -> viewer.canvas.size

# Scene Model
viewer.camera -> viewer.scene.camera
viewer.axes -> viewer.scene.overlays.axes
  
 Removal of translation code 
 Several years ago, we started working on implementing localization machinery
into napari. Unfortunately, this work has been sitting unfinished and unused,
while making maintaining napari harder. Given the extra maintenance burden
without benefit, we made the difficult decision to remove it from our codebase
( #8935 ), with the hope that in
the future we might restart this effort with a better plan. 
 We do aim to revisit when napari's foundations are more solid, but for now,
 napari.utils.translations  is deprecated. If you have this code in your
codebase: 
  from napari.utils import translations as trans
  
 please remove it. (For now,  trans._()  is a no-op.)

title: In vivo Study of the Effect of Composition and Implantation Site on Scaffold Degradation Rate: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) 50:50+20wt%TaOx, Intramuscular
journal: Hix, Jeremy M.L., Troia, Arianna, Shapiro, Erik
text:
In vivo Study of the Effect of Composition and Implantation Site on Scaffold Degradation Rate: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) 50:50+20wt%TaOx, Intramuscular.  Tissue engineering devices stabilize wounds, then degrade. However, published degradation rates often conflict. Incorporating monitoring functionality into devices allows real-time assessment of degradation and failure, but requires contrast agents, as polymer devices are invisible to most medical imaging modalities. Therefore, computed tomography (CT)-visible composite scaffolds were created from 5-20 wt% tantalum oxide (TaO x ) nanoparticles in polymers with distinct degradation profiles: polycaprolactone, poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) 85:15 and PLGA 50:50, representing slow, medium and fast degrading materials. Scaffolds, mimicking biomedical devices, were implanted into mice intramuscularly or intraperitoneally, and monitored via CT over 20 weeks. Scaffold degradation profile was dictated by polymer matrix, regardless of nanoparticle addition. Foreign body response was dependent on implant site and in mid-degrading composites degradation rates transitioned from linear degradation intramuscularly to exponential degradation intraperitoneally. Nanoparticle excretion via liver and spleen lagged polymer degradation. Overall, real time tracking of device behavior was demonstrated, advancing an era of personalized medicine. Published as: Pawelec, K.M., Hix, J.M.L., Troia, A.  et al.  In vivo study of the effect of composition and implantation site on scaffold degradation rate.  Commun Mater  (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-026-01308-5 
 This dataset contains longitudinal microCT scans of poly(lactide-co-glycolide)(PLGA) 50:50+20wt% TaOx, implanted intramuscularly. Each individual in the group (n=6) was scanned 25 mm field of view (4 min total scan time) at 50 μm resolution, centered on the implanted scaffold. After all acquisitions, individual scaffolds were again sub-reconstructed using the Quantum GX software to 12 µm resolution.

title: Pregnancy-Wise Leakage-Controlled Multi-Representation Fusion for Classifying Early- and Later-Recorded Electrohysterographic Recordings Using Wavelet Scalograms
journal: Sağlam, Ahmet, Şentürk, Ümit, Yücedağ, İbrahim
text: Pregnancy-Wise Leakage-Controlled Multi-Representation Fusion for Classifying Early- and Later-Recorded Electrohysterographic Recordings Using Wavelet Scalograms. Code associated with a pregnancy-wise leakage-controlled CNN–Transformer framework for classifying early- and later-recorded electrohysterographic recordings in ICEHG DS using S1, S2, S3, and RGB wavelet-scalogram representations and probability-level fusion. The endpoint is recording period, not preterm-birth prediction, delivery-outcome prediction, gestational-age estimation, or clinical diagnosis.

title: What Belongs in the Tool and Which Behaviour Must Be Taught:
text:
What Belongs in the Tool and Which Behaviour Must Be Taught:.     Summary for the reader who has to decide  
 Each point summarises a chapter or a thematic block and closes with its own reliability mark and its principal source. 
  ●          Two educational questions are routinely merged into one, and the merger makes the harder of the two disappear : how to converse with these systems, which can largely be answered with a pedagogy that the caring professions already possess, and how to preserve the capacity to work without them, which no curriculum answers today {I,  MDU-12  and this document, ch. 1}. 
  ●          The problem grows worse as the systems improve , because an unreliable system keeps vigilance alive whereas a reliable system removes the occasions for checking, and not checking a system that is almost always right is rational cognitive economy and not negligence {P,  AIRA-KRIF-02a  §1.2 and  AIRA-HAL-04  A}. 
  ●          The machine is strong on exactness and is blind to pertinence and to feasibility , and it does not signal that it lacks the knowledge of the case on which pertinence depends; verification therefore migrates towards what is verifiable, and a badly designed educational programme certifies instead of protecting {I,  AIRA-KRIF-02a  §3.3}. 
  ●          The oracle position is a fact about the chain and not an attitude : whoever speaks last before the action is an oracle irrespective of their own accuracy, and a sceptical professional who acts on an output with nothing intervening downstream is treating it exactly as such {I,  AIRA-KRIF-02a  §1.1}. 
  ●          The pipeline that used to produce competence has been interrupted, and this is measured : unassisted adenoma detection fell from 28.4 to 22.4 per cent after continuous exposure to assistance, with converging findings in radiology and in pathology, while the occupational effect is a post that is never advertised rather than a dismissal, and is therefore invisible {T, Budzyń 2025;  MDU-04 }. 
  ●          The structure of the problem orients the solution, and a well-defined problem is already close to its solution because it supplies the criteria by which to judge it : formulating the question well is not a preliminary precaution but the greater part of the work, and it is for this reason that Chapter 4 opens from there instead of arriving at it in the end {L, maxim attributed to Einstein, an attribution that is widespread and has no ascertained source; this document, §4.1}. 
  ●          Conversing with these systems is a communication competence and not a technical competence , so what is needed is the deliberate transfer of an existing pedagogy plus compensation for three signals that a machine interlocutor does not give: it does not say that it lacks your context, it does not offer you resistance, and its fluency carries no information whatever about its confidence {I, this document, ch. 4}. 
  ●          The danger is not that the machine mirrors the starting position of the person asking, because it is also able to comment, to object and to show the holes in the reasoning ; the danger is that one has no way of knowing which of the two things one has received, given that elaborate confirmation and criticism arrive with the very same fluency, which is once again the third missing signal {I, this document, §4.1 and §4.2}. 
  ●          What is taught must be moves and not scripts , because a formulation repeated identically becomes liturgy, and prescribing four sentences to a profession produces exactly the lexical homogenisation that the document exists in order to prevent {I,  AIRA-SKL-01  and  MDU-13 }. 
  ●          The five groups of actors differ by institutional defences and not by fragility, and each of them holds a resource that the machine does not have ; the question is not how to protect the weak but how to prevent each group from losing what it alone possesses {I,  AIRA-HAL-10  §10.2}. 
  ●          A fifth group of actors is added here, the multi-stakeholder steering group , whose unit is not the person but the table, whose error manifests itself as distributed distortion visible only in aggregate, and which is the only group that has authority over the resources that all the other recommendations presuppose {I,  KRIF-01a  §3.1 and  PAP-01  §6, extended here}. 
  ●          Tables fail in four ways, which here are no longer analytical distinctions but predictions each with its own observable : ratification, in which the output becomes the agenda and which is checked by counting how many alternatives appear in the minutes before a written proposal reaches the table; the prevalence of the lowest posture, which is checked by looking at who questions the material brought by someone else, and how many times; and the drift of the shared lexicon, which is checked by comparing, a year later, the glossary of the table with that of the system it uses {P, this document, §8.4}. 
  ●          The third and the fourth mode are the same failure seen twice , because sublimation without re-particularisation is the case in which the second movement does not occur, and what distinguishes the fault from correct functioning is precisely whether or not that movement is accomplished; the pair is not ours but is described in  IAL-21 , Chapter 2, as a bidirectional process performed by the artificial intelligence {L, single source and not independent}. 
  ●          Ratification has a pre-computational ancestor inside the corpus itself , the illusion of consensus described in  IAL-21 , in which participants believe they have agreed while they have merely found formulations that each of them interprets in their own way; it should therefore be presented as the amplified form of a failure already documented with no machine at all, whose antidote — AI as a systematic explorer of alternatives — simply remains inactive in ratification {L,  IAL-21 }. 
  ●          Ownership of the objective function is the non-delegable core , and it requires three instituted ingredients — a named holder, a calendar cadence, and a flow of data that measures the effects of the criterion rather than the functioning of the system; in their absence the "what counts" has been delegated to inertia {P,  KRIF-01b  §2.5 and §9.2}. 
  ●          What can be made invariant is to be built into the tool and what cannot belongs to education , and this is no longer an inference: a randomised study manipulated exactly this variable — same technology, same task, same students, the only difference being what was written in the system prompt — finding a fall of 17 per cent on the unassisted test in the arm without protections and a non-significant fall of 0.4 per cent in the protected arm {P, Bastani and colleagues 2024; this document, §12.2}. 
  ●          The sites of embedding are four and they form a cascade : the posture that sits in the generalist model, that is, asking before answering, declaring assumptions and not reassuring about what cannot be excluded; the supra-local reference configuration, national or international, produced as a public good for specific tasks and objectives; the local customisation of the instance, that is, this health district, these care pathways, these resources; and finally the loaded knowledge base, that is, the k-file, the glossary and the agreed core {P, this document, ch. 12}. 
  ●          The descent along the cascade cannot, however, be complete , because the limit set out in Chapter 2 holds for the configuration as well: a national configuration does not know this health district any more than the model knows this particular patient, and there always remains a residue to be configured locally and, beneath it, a residue that cannot be configured at all and is left to education {I, this document, §12.2}. 
  ●          The knowledge manager is not a sixth group of actors but a role internal to the steering group , because he or she has no institutional defence of their own and is rather the custodian of the resource of the fifth group, that is, of the knowledge distributed among the members and possessed by none of them, which the knowledge manager makes explicit, curates and loads into the tool {I, this document, §8.6}. 
  ●          The risk attaching to the knowledge manager is not the oracle but imitation without understanding , because he or she does not speak last and is not the only one to have seen, whereas the table may copy their formulations instead of learning their moves; the role is moreover transitory by design, with a sequence of led, co-led, autonomous, whose exit is to be dated in the initial mandate {I, this document, §8.6}. 
  ●          Seven arrangements constitute the educational equipment , and the three that have no current equivalent are those that answer the second question: seeded-error cases, recurrent practice without the system, and reconstructed apprenticeship {P on the evidence for the first two;  MDU-09 }. 
  ●          Education cannot supply time, mandate or staffing, nor can it heal the divergence between who pays and who benefits , and saying so openly is the defence against the use of education as an alibi in place of organisational change {I,  MDU-09 }. 
  ●          For four groups of actors time works in their favour, and this document will age into being the description of native functions; for citizens it works against them , because a system that is more fluent, warmer and more personalised aggravates the compensatory oracle, and the regulatory architecture presupposes the opposite {I,  AIRA-HAL-08  K}.

chimera-agent-training-data.   CHIMERA-Agent Training Data  
 This archive contains the training release for the CHIMERA-Agent challenge. 
 For full challenge details, visit:  https://chimera-agent.grand-challenge.org/  
  Dataset structure  
 The archive is organized into three task folders. Each task contains one folder per patient. 
  Task 1 files:  
 
 prostate-biopsy-decision-clinical-data.json 
 structured-prompt.json 
 prostate-modality-level-neural-representations.json 
 prostate-biopsy-decision.json 
 prostate-biopsy-decision-reasoning.json 
 
  Task 2 files:  
 
 prostate-treatment-decision-clinical-data.json 
 structured-prompt.json 
 prostate-modality-level-neural-representations.json 
 prostate-treatment-decision.json 
 prostate-treatment-decision-reasoning.json 
 
  Task 3 files:  
 
 prostate-time-to-recurrence-or-last-follow-up-clinical-data.json 
 structured-prompt.json 
 prostate-modality-level-neural-representations.json 
 prostate-time-to-recurrence-or-last-follow-up.json 
 
 Ground-truth labels and reference reasoning are currently available for  91 Task 1 cases and 72 Task 2 cases . Task 3 includes ground-truth labels for  75 cases  and no reference reasoning. 
 Task 1 and Task 2 reference-reasoning files include a  reveal_sequence  field indicating which clinical-data sections were accessed during the decision. For Task 2,  reveal_sequence  information is currently unavailable, so the field is represented as an empty list ( [] ). For details, visit:  https://chimera-agent.grand-challenge.org/data-sources-and-imaging/  
  Structured prompt updates  
 
  Task 1:  Biopsy- and pathology-derived fields ( bx_isup ,  bx_gl_prim ,  bx_gl_sec ,  bx_gl_tert ,  bx_isup_pred ,  cores_positive ,  cores_total ,  max_core_pct ,  growth_pattern ,  high_risk_patterns ,  pni ,  lvi , and  tumor_location ) were removed from  structured-prompt.json  to avoid data leakage into the biopsy-decision task. 
  Task 1 and Task 2:  The  id  field was removed from  structured-prompt.json , as it enabled linking the same patient across the two tasks. 
 
 ⚠️  Important:  The updated  structured-prompt.json  schema is the one that will be used for the validation and test input files. 
  Modality-level Neural representation format  
 Each prostate-modality-level-neural-representations.json file follows this structure: 
 { "MRI image": [[...]], "Biopsy slide": [[...], [...], [...]], "Prostatectomy slide": [[...], [...], [...]] } 
 Missing modalities are represented as  [] .

title: Dataset for: 3' mRNA-seq dataset of human chondrocytes treated with caspase-1 and -8 inhibitors under osteoarthritis-like conditions
journal: Vesela, Barbora, Zapletalova, Martina, Pasoldt, Anja
text: Dataset for: 3' mRNA-seq dataset of human chondrocytes treated with caspase-1 and -8 inhibitors under osteoarthritis-like conditions.   About 655 million persons worldwide are affected by osteoarthritis (OA), associated with excruciating chronic pain and disability in the elderly. Inflammation and cell death are two key events in OA and also key canonical functions of caspases. Since caspases play an important role in modulating inflammation, caspase inhibitors have been widely utilized to study diseases involving inflammation in animal models and clinical trials. Among these, key caspases, which are responsible for activation of the corresponding pathways include caspase-8 for the receptor mediated apoptotic pathway and caspase-1 as the key inflammatory caspase being involved in OA pathogenesis.   OA- and non-OA chondrocytes were treated with caspase-1 and -8 inhibitors and TNF-  a  .   RNA was isolated after 3 days from three biological replicates (n=3) of each group an  d processed for single-end RNA sequencing (1 x 114 bp). Data was pre-processed and analyzed with R programming language v4.2.2. Downstream analysis included identification of differentially expressed genes providing a comprehensive overview of unique and shared transcriptional changes in both OA and non-OA cohorts.
